chapters.title: Chapter 2: What You Give Up and What You Keep

lessons.title: Section 80C, 80D and NPS: The Big Deductions Explained

children.text: Every January, HR sends the same email: submit your investment proofs or extra TDS will be cut from your February and March salary. Offices fill with people buying last-minute ELSS units and insurance policies they do not understand. Almost all of that panic is about three deductions: Section 80C, NPS and Section 80D. In the old regime they can shave lakhs off your taxable income. In the new regime, with one exception, they are worth nothing.

body.text: A deduction does not save you the amount you invest. It saves you that amount multiplied by your marginal tax rate. ₹1.5 lakh in 80C saves ₹46,800 at the 30% slab, but only ₹7,800 at the 5% slab.

body.caption: The 1.04 adds the 4% cess you also avoid. Example: ₹1,50,000 × 30% × 1.04 = ₹46,800.

children.text: Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 80C of the 1961 Act) is one shared bucket with a ₹1,50,000 annual cap. Many different payments count towards it, but together they can never exceed ₹1.5 lakh. It is available only in the old regime.

body.text: Check your payslip before buying anything. If your basic salary is ₹50,000 a month, your 12% EPF contribution is ₹6,000 a month, or ₹72,000 a year. Nearly half your 80C bucket is already full without you lifting a finger.

body.title: How Much 80C Room Is Left?
body.prompt: Kavya, a teacher at a private school in Jaipur, has a basic salary of ₹40,000 a month with 12% EPF deducted. She pays a ₹25,000 annual LIC premium and ₹40,000 in tuition fees for her son. How much more can she invest this year and still get an 80C deduction?
body.explanation: EPF is 12% of ₹40,000, which is ₹4,800 a month or ₹57,600 a year. Add the ₹25,000 LIC premium and ₹40,000 tuition fees for a total of ₹1,22,600. The cap is ₹1,50,000, so ₹27,400 of room remains.

children.text: NPS: Three Layers, and One Survives in the New Regime

markDefs.definition: The National Pension System, a government-regulated retirement scheme overseen by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA).

children.text: deductions sit in Section 124 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 80CCD of the 1961 Act). They come in three layers, and people routinely confuse them. The distinction matters, because the third layer is one of the very few deductions the new regime still allows.

cells: Up to 10% of basic plus DA, inside the ₹1.5 lakh 80C cap
10% of basic plus DA in old regime (14% for government employees); 14% in new regime

body.label: Maximum old regime deduction for your own NPS money
body.context: ₹1,50,000 inside the 80C bucket plus ₹50,000 under 80CCD(1B), but only if nothing else is using the 80C bucket.

body.text: NPS money is designed for retirement. Most of the corpus stays locked until 60, and part of it must be used to buy an annuity that pays taxable pension income. Do not put ₹50,000 into NPS purely to claim 80CCD(1B) unless you are comfortable with that lock-in. Also note that employer contributions to EPF, NPS and superannuation above ₹7.5 lakh a year in total are taxed as a perquisite.

body.title: Name the NPS Layer
body.textWithBlank: The extra ₹50,000 deduction for your own NPS contribution, over and above the ₹1.5 lakh 80C limit, is known by its 1961 Act reference as Section 80CCD(___).
body.explanation: 80CCD(1B) is the extra ₹50,000 for your own contribution and is old regime only. Do not confuse it with 80CCD(2), the employer contribution deduction that survives in the new regime.

children.text: Section 126 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 80D of the 1961 Act) covers health insurance premiums. It has two separate buckets, one for you, your spouse and your children, and one for your parents. Each bucket has its own cap, which doubles if the oldest insured person in it is a senior citizen. Premiums must be paid by any mode other than cash.

cells: Up to ₹5,000, within the bucket caps above (cash allowed)
Up to ₹5,000, within the bucket caps above (cash allowed)

body.title: Work Out Rohit's 80D
body.question: Rohit, 45, lives in Lucknow. He pays ₹22,000 for a family floater covering himself, his wife and his daughter, spends ₹4,000 on a health check-up for himself, and pays ₹55,000 for his parents' policy. Both parents are over 60. What is his maximum 80D deduction?
body.explanation: His own bucket is ₹22,000 plus ₹4,000, which is ₹26,000, capped at ₹25,000 because nobody in it is a senior. The parents' bucket is ₹55,000, capped at ₹50,000 because they are seniors. Total: ₹75,000.

children.text: What the Big Three Are Actually Worth

body.caption: Tax Saved by Maxing Each Deduction in the Old Regime (Including 4% Cess)

body.text: Even a taxpayer in the 30% slab who maxes out all three saves ₹85,800. Now remember Lesson 3: at ₹15 lakh of taxable income, the old regime's slab tax is ₹1,57,500 higher than the new regime's. The big three alone rarely close that gap. That is why HRA and home loan interest, covered in the next lesson, usually decide the outcome.

children.text: What Happens to All This in the New Regime

body.title: New Regime: Lost vs Still Available

columns.label: No deduction in the new regime
points: 80C: EPF, PPF, ELSS, life insurance, tuition fees, home loan principal
80CCD(1) and 80CCD(1B): your own NPS contribution
80D: health insurance premiums and check-ups

columns.label: Still true in the new regime
points: 80CCD(2): employer NPS contribution up to 14% of basic plus DA
PPF and SSY interest and maturity remain tax-free
EPF interest stays tax-free within the usual limits

body.title: Deepak Wants to Cancel Everything
body.scenario: Deepak, 29, is a data engineer in Bengaluru on ₹20 lakh and has moved to the new regime. He contributes ₹1,00,000 a year to PPF, runs a ₹5,000 monthly ELSS SIP and pays ₹18,000 for a health insurance policy. Since none of these give him a deduction any more, he plans to stop all three and spend the money.
body.prompt: Which of his decisions make sense, and which are mistakes?
body.modelAnswer: Health insurance is the clear mistake. He bought it to protect against hospital bills, not to save tax, and a single hospitalisation in a Bengaluru private hospital can cost far more than years of premiums. Keep it. PPF still has tax-free interest and maturity in both regimes, so if he wants a safe, long-term debt allocation it remains useful. He should decide on its merits, not on the lost deduction. The ELSS SIP no longer earns a deduction, so he could reasonably redirect future instalments to a diversified equity fund or index fund with no lock-in. Units he already holds stay locked for 3 years from each purchase date. What he should not do is stop saving altogether. The new regime lowered his tax. It did not lower his need to invest.

cards.definition: ₹1,50,000 a year, shared across EPF, PPF, ELSS, life insurance, tuition fees, home loan principal and more. Old regime only.
Extra ₹50,000 for your own NPS contribution, over and above 80C. Old regime only.
Employer NPS contribution. 14% of basic plus DA in the new regime. Available in both regimes.
Two: self, spouse and children; and parents. ₹25,000 each, rising to ₹50,000 where a senior citizen is covered.
Amount claimed × marginal slab rate × 1.04. Worth far more in the 30% slab than the 5% slab.

body.title: Build Your Big Three Worksheet
steps: Find your annual EPF contribution on your payslip or the EPFO passbook
List every other 80C payment you already make and total it, capped at ₹1,50,000
Check whether you contribute to NPS yourself, and whether your employer contributes under 80CCD(2)
Collect health insurance premium receipts for your own policy and your parents' policy
Multiply your total by your marginal slab rate and 1.04 to see what the old regime deductions are really worth

points: A deduction saves tax at your marginal rate plus cess, not rupee for rupee.
80C, now Section 123, is one ₹1.5 lakh bucket, and your EPF contribution often fills much of it already.
NPS has three layers: 80CCD(1) inside 80C, 80CCD(1B) for an extra ₹50,000, and 80CCD(2) for employer contributions.
Only the employer NPS deduction, 80CCD(2), survives in the new regime, at up to 14% of basic plus DA.
80D, now Section 126, has separate buckets for your family and your parents, each doubling when a senior is covered.
Maxing all three saves at most ₹85,800 even at the 30% slab, which is rarely enough on its own to make the old regime win.
